A specific, provocative idea: a saccharine storybook world (rainbows, swans, peacocks, seals) turned against grimy old mechanical engines, which are shown flying, being batted away and swarming. The tone carries the message.

Type is built into the world instead of laid on top of it. Letters appear as topiary, as eyes on a peacock's tail and as balls balanced by seals, so each word belongs to a different creature and staging.

Every frame has a different set-up, scale and camera: a wide establishing landscape, a mid shot with a flamingo swinging a bat, a frontal circus line-up, and a crowd scene with particles and smoke. That shows real choreography across the film.
The rendering deliberately clashes materials: soft, over-lit, candy-coloured pastoral against heavy, rusted, textured metal. The sickly-sweet palette is a choice, not a default.
Lots of character animation, including a bunny, a flamingo, seals and deer, with weight and comic timing implied across the frames.
gaps: The pastoral is deliberately twee, but some background elements (trees, clouds) look stock. Pushing them to match the detail of the engines would raise the whole image.
Central compositions like the seal line-up are close to symmetrical and posed. One or two more dynamic, off-axis camera moves would help.
This is the benchmark entry. The gap left is only finish: the uniform bright light flattens depth in places where a stronger key light could sculpt the forms.

tells: A title-sequence chase told in silhouette. The credits are staged inside the action: on an arch sign, painted on the ground in a pool of lamplight, and riding a vortex.
A bold palette that changes scene by scene: dusty rose, nocturnal violet and green, acid lime with a yellow spiral, and teal dusk. Each frame works as a poster.
Strong cinematic staging: an overhead dutch angle with a pool of light, deep perspective, and characters thrown across a hypnotic spiral. The editing clearly varies scale and point of view.
Typography with a period point of view: chunky slab and sans credits set in perspective, with lettering integrated into the image.
Paper grain and print-like texture give a deliberate retro-graphic finish.
gaps: The vocabulary of silhouette-chase titles (Saul Bass, Catch Me If You Can) is well trodden. Compared with A, the core idea is homage rather than invention.
The credit type style changes from frame to frame (slab on the arch, flat sans elsewhere). A tighter typographic system would read as more authored.
The light is mostly flat graphic fills. The one frame with motivated lamplight is the strongest, and using that more widely would add depth.

tells: Rich, tactile, bespoke 3D materials: translucent waxy hands, coral-like growths, green mesh fabric, hair-fine fibres, glassy tubes and beaded clusters. These are not stock primitives.
An unusual, deliberate palette: salmon and coral against icy blue, olive and bottle green, and a mauve dusk.
Each frame has a distinct world and scale, from a macro tangle to a volcanic landscape with an eruption.
The labels ('Boldtron', 'Medusa Lab') suggest an anthology or reel of artist segments, which explains the variety but weakens the through-line.
gaps: No single idea ties the frames together. It reads as a reel of beautiful renders rather than a film with a concept like A's.
The type is small bold grotesk labels dropped in a corner with no relation to the image. They need integration, scale or a typographic idea.
Composition leans on dense, centred material spectacle. Clear focal hierarchy and choreography that links shot to shot are missing.

defects: The last ~2 s (8–11 s, per-second change 4.2/3.9) is a near-static hold on the finished poster. Only the polyhedron keeps drifting, so the ending reads as dead air rather than a designed settle.
Intermediate frames are badly framed: 'MPEST' is cropped at the left edge, and the red disc and halftone card cover the moon mid-move. These are push-in states, not composed beats.

The halftone polyhedron's silhouette changes between frames that are 1/6 s apart. It reads as a randomly deforming lo-poly shape rather than a recognisable object (ship, island, cloud), so the eye has nowhere to land.
Motion runs in alternating bursts and lulls (75/6/64/67/15/64/10/60). Elements arrive one at a time on a slide-and-settle, with no overlap or follow-through between layers.
The audio's biggest moment, a broadband noise burst around 5.8–6.1 s, has no clearly matching visual impact. Per-second change in that window is no higher than in the earlier cuts.
Typography is a stock condensed grotesk on a yellow tape strip plus a mono credit line. It appears with a plain slide and carries no motion or meaning of its own.
The 3.5 s longest shot and 1.55 s median fail the pace benchmark. Both are dominated by holds, not by too many cuts.
gaps: Choreography: top studios would build the collage as one continuous, overlapping physical gesture, with paper flutter, drop shadows that lift and land, and torn edges catching air, ideally with the sea turning to storm as the layers pile up. Here it is sequential slide-ins with linear-feeling camera pushes, and the tempest itself never appears.

Sound: there is a sustained low synth bed plus an accelerating tick riser into a white-noise swell, which is a stock build. Missing are paper and tape foley, wind and sea texture, and transients locked to each layer landing. The release after 6 s goes back to the static bed instead of resolving.

Finish and concept: the paper grain, torn deckle edges and clean halftone hold up at 100%, but the piece is a layout that assembles itself, not an idea. The ending hold, cropped intermediate frames, the meaningless polyhedron and type with no meaning keep it at good-template level rather than award level.
